newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt finances finally start to improve.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt finances finally start to improve.

text.p: The Australian government's finances are showing belated improvement.
The stubborn refusal of revenue to lift towards the 1996/97 target is giving way to some tentative signs of improvement.
The rolling-12-month underlying deficit, which is largely free of seasonal effects, fell to A$10.7 billion in September from A$13.1 billion in August.
Before the September data, the underlying budget deficit was showing an obstinately flat trendline around A$12 billion. (See the table at the foot of this report.)

But even now it remains higher than the freak A$10.3 billion recorded for the 12 months to June 1996 -- a result which was much better than the surrounding data but which coincidentally goes into the record books as the official figure for 1995/96.
And the latest 12-month number is still nowhere near the A$5.6 billion that the budget papers forecast for the year to June 1997. The budget has nine months in which to close that gap.
Revenue, not shown in the table, was A$121.7 billion for the 12 months to September, a hefty A$2 billion improvement on the A$119.7 billion recorded in the two previous months.
Twelve-month revenue is supposed to reach A$130.2 billion by June.
The rolling-12-month analysis largely overcomes strong seasonality that defeats most methods of assessing the budget's current condition.
CORRECTION
Readers may be surprised to hear that government finances will improve by fully A$5.9 billion later today or on Wednesday.

More accurately, the Finance Department will correct an unfortunate error of that magnitude on the front page of the September Commonwealth Government Statement of Financial Transactions (CFT), which was issued on Friday.
The September monthly underlying deficit was shown on the document at exactly A$6.300 billion, although the true result was $400 million.
The department mistakenly deducted net advances (which were minus A$3.35 billion -- the Commonwealth Bank share revenue) instead of adding them.
Interestingly, that should have given them a A$6.3 billion surplus, which would have raised a few eyebrows, but they labelled it as a deficit instead.
That should have raised eyebrows anyway, but it seems it has taken four days for this rather impressive error to come to light.
The error did not affect the financial-year-to-date result.
